subtype: Warm welcome to a lonely person [Receiver]
passage:
Rajma-chawal, Himani. That's how it started, with a plate of rajma-chawal.
I'm Urmila, and I'd been in Delhi three weeks for my master's. My Nani had died in August, and I cried in the hostel bathroom most nights. Then two girls at the library said, "There's a free dinner Friday, come, we're all a bit far from home." They remembered my name the next day. They hugged me. When I mentioned Nani, one of them cried with me.
I honestly can't tell you what they believed. I never really listened to the talks. I went back for the people, for being wanted.
It was the retreat that woke me up. They said, "Skip your cousin's engagement, this weekend is more important for your growth." I said no. The hugs got noticeably cooler after that.
That's when I understood what the dinner had been for.

qa.q: What did the two girls at the library invite Urmila to?
qa.a: They invited Urmila to a free dinner on Friday.

qa.q: What was Urmila really hoping to feel by going back again and again?
qa.a: Urmila was grieving Nani and lonely in a new city, so the pull was the warmth and the feeling of being wanted, not the beliefs.

qa.q: Which moment in Urmila's story revealed what the group wanted?
qa.a: Being told to skip a cousin's engagement for the retreat, and then feeling the hugs cool after saying no, showed Urmila that the warmth came with conditions.

qa.q: How might Himani feel hearing this story?
qa.a: Himani might feel sad that Urmila was so alone in those first weeks, and glad that Urmila held on to family instead of the retreat.

grounding: A grieving student new to Delhi is welcomed by friendly people with dinners and hugs, and the pull is the feeling of being wanted, not their beliefs.

subtype: Warm welcome to a lonely person [Receiver]
passage:
I share a hostel room with Yamini, so I saw how fast it happened.
She arrived in July, quiet, with a framed photo of her father on her desk. He had died the year before; she told me that on the second night, and then nothing more for weeks.
In September some older students started inviting her out. First a potluck. Then a "sharing circle" on Sundays. Then a weekend trip to a farmhouse. She came back glowing. "They remembered my birthday, Sarita," she said. "Nobody here even knew it."
What struck me was that she never once told me what the group believed. Only who hugged her, who texted, who saved her a seat.
I can't know what's in her head. But I noticed I had never asked about her birthday either.
Last Sunday I asked her to come to the market with me instead. She hesitated, then said yes.

qa.q: What did Yamini say the group remembered?
qa.a: Yamini said they remembered her birthday.

qa.q: What does Yamini's glowing after the farmhouse trip suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests Yamini felt wanted and less alone after losing her father, even though Sarita admits not knowing exactly what is in her head.

qa.q: What small step did Sarita take, and why might it help?
qa.a: Sarita invited Yamini to the market; offering ordinary friendship means the group is not the only place Yamini feels remembered.

qa.q: Why might Yamini talk about people rather than ideas?
qa.a: The pull for Yamini seems to be belonging, not doctrine; being hugged, texted and saved a seat matters more to someone grieving than any belief.

grounding: Sarita watches Yamini, a grieving student in the same hostel room, drawn to a group by instant warmth, noticing that Yamini speaks only of being wanted, never of what the group believes.

subtype: Warm welcome to a lonely person [Receiver]
passage:
First week, a Monday: Sarika ate dinner alone in the hostel mess for the fifth day running, scrolling photos of her friends back in Guwahati. Nobody in Bengaluru knew her name.
Second week, a Saturday: a smiling senior, Sudha, sat beside her in the library. "You look like you need a proper meal. Come for our Sunday lunch." Sarika went. Twenty people clapped when she walked in. Someone had already learnt she liked fish curry. They called each other "family". She laughed more that afternoon than in the whole month before.
Fourth week, a Sunday: riding back in Sudha's car after the third lunch, Sarika realised she couldn't say what the group actually believed. Something about "the path". She didn't really care. She only knew that on Sundays, for a few hours, she stopped feeling like a stranger. When her mother called that night and asked about the lunches, Sarika answered quickly and changed the subject.

qa.q: What had someone already learnt about Sarika at the first Sunday lunch?
qa.a: Someone had already learnt she liked fish curry.

qa.q: Why did Sarika keep going back to the Sunday lunches?
qa.a: Sarika felt lonely in a new city, and at the lunches she felt wanted and stopped feeling like a stranger; the beliefs hardly mattered to her.

qa.q: What could Sarika do before going deeper into the group?
qa.a: Ask Sudha plainly what the group believes and expects, talk openly with her mother about the lunches, and keep making other friends at college.

qa.q: How might Sarika's mother see the quick change of subject on the phone?
qa.a: Her mother may sense something is being held back and feel a little worried, even without knowing what the lunches are.

grounding: Shows a student new to a city drawn in by a warm Sunday lunch where the pull is feeling wanted, not the group's beliefs.

subtype: Warm welcome to a lonely person [Receiver]
passage:
Abhinav, you've been going to those Saturday meetings since your grandfather passed. I'm not going to scold you. Let me just tell you a story.
When I was twenty, my father died in March, and by June I was a ghost at college. Then a girl from my hostel, all smiles, took my hand and brought me to a "study circle". They hugged me at the door. They brought me tea without asking. For the first time in months, when I skipped a day, someone said, "We missed you, Swati."
I didn't care what they taught. I cared that they wanted me.
It was my cousin Hema who noticed. She came to the hostel, sat on my bed and said, "I'm glad you have people. Will they still want you if you ask questions?" So at the next meeting I asked one question. The smiles went thin.
That was my turning point. The warmth had been real, but it came with a price.

qa.q: When did Swati's father die?
qa.a: Swati's father died in March.

qa.q: Why was young Swati drawn to the study circle?
qa.a: Young Swati was grieving and lonely, and felt wanted when they hugged at the door and said 'We missed you'; the teachings hardly mattered.

qa.q: What was the turning point inside the story?
qa.a: Asking one question at the next meeting, as Hema suggested; the thin smiles showed the welcome depended on not questioning.

qa.q: How did Hema see what was happening to Swati?
qa.a: Hema was glad Swati had people but worried about the price, so Hema asked a gentle question instead of scolding.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how, while grieving at twenty, a group's warm welcome hooked her through the feeling of being wanted.

subtype: Warm welcome to a lonely person [Receiver]
passage:
The hostel emptied for the Diwali break, and Nazia's train ticket home to Lucknow was still waitlisted. On the second silent evening, rain hammering the tin roof of the canteen, she was the only one eating.
Lalit, a cheerful volunteer who had been handing out leaflets near the library all month, shook out his umbrella and sat opposite. "Nobody should be alone during the holidays. We're doing a free weekend retreat. Food, music, good people. Bus leaves at seven."
She hesitated. She didn't even know what the retreat was about.
"Doesn't matter," Lalit said, smiling. "You'll feel at home."
At the retreat that night, thirty strangers learnt her name within an hour. Someone wrapped a shawl around her shoulders. For the first time since she'd come to Delhi, she fell asleep without that heavy lump in her chest.
The next morning her phone showed two missed calls from Ammi. She had forgotten to tell anyone where she was.

qa.q: What time did the retreat bus leave?
qa.a: The bus leaves at seven.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling that first night at the retreat?
qa.a: Nazia felt comforted and at home for once, falling asleep without the heavy lump of loneliness in her chest.

qa.q: What would be a wise first step the next morning?
qa.a: Call Ammi back, say exactly where she is, and find out what the retreat is really about before staying longer.

qa.q: How might Ammi feel after two unanswered calls?
qa.a: Ammi would likely feel anxious, not knowing where Nazia was during the holidays.

grounding: Shows a lonely student stranded over the holidays accepting a retreat invitation and feeling instant belonging without knowing what the group is.

subtype: Warm welcome to a lonely person [Receiver]
passage: Three weeks after moving to Pune for her master's, and two months after Nani died, Vinita still ate dinner alone in her PG room most nights. So when Pradeep, a smiling boy from her statistics class, said, "We have a small community dinner on Fridays, very chill, come," she almost cried with relief. The flat in Kothrud was warm and smelled of dal. Twelve people knew her name within an hour. A girl hugged her at the door. Someone had saved her a plate. Nobody asked about grades or salaries; they asked how she was, and waited for the answer. There was a short talk about finding your true family, which she half listened to. What she remembered was the feeling, like being wrapped in a blanket. In the auto home she realised she didn't know the group's name, or who ran it. She pushed the thought away. They had already added her to three chats.

qa.q: Where was the Friday dinner held?
qa.a: In a flat in Kothrud.

qa.q: Why did the group feel so good to Vinita?
qa.a: Vinita felt lonely and full of grief, so being welcomed, hugged and asked how she was felt like relief, like being wrapped in a blanket.

qa.q: What could Vinita do before going deeper?
qa.a: She could find out the group's name and who runs it, keep up her other friendships, and notice whether questions are welcome.

qa.q: How might Pradeep see inviting Vinita?
qa.a: Pradeep may genuinely think he is being kind to a lonely classmate, whatever the group's aims, which is part of why the welcome feels sincere.

grounding: Shows a lonely, grieving student invited to a warm group dinner and pulled in by the feeling of being wanted rather than by any ideas.
